insolence

IN-suh-lens -- from Latin insolentia, from insolens ('unaccustomed, arrogant'), in- ('not') + solere ('to be accustomed'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Insolence is disrespectful and rude behavior, especially toward someone in a position of authority.

During the trial, the defendant's open insolence -- interrupting the proceedings and scoffing at every ruling -- nearly resulted in a contempt charge.

Example

The knight's insolence toward the queen -- refusing to bow and openly mocking her decree in front of the court -- led to his banishment.

That open, deliberate disrespect directed at someone who is owed basic courtesy -- a teacher, a boss, an elder -- is exactly what insolence describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disrespect: Disrespect is any failure to show the regard a person deserves -- it can be as mild as ignoring a greeting, and it can pass between equals. Insolence sharpens it into something bolder: open, mocking rudeness aimed upward at a person in authority who is owed courtesy.

defiance: Defiance is open refusal to obey -- ignoring an order or breaking a rule on purpose. Insolence needs no order to refuse: it is rude, mocking behavior toward a person in authority. A soldier who refuses a direct command shows defiance; one who obeys it while smirking at the officer shows insolence.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deference: respectful submission to someone's wishes or authority

courtesy: polite, respectful behavior toward others

Where it sits · how brazen the disrespect is — impertinence → insolence → impudence

impertinence vs. insolence: Impertinence is milder than insolence: a waiter's impertinent correction earns a stern look, while open insolence toward the manager could cost him the job on the spot.

impudence vs. insolence: Impudence is stronger than insolence: insolence is contemptuous rudeness toward authority, but impudence goes further into shameless brazenness, like propping your feet up on the principal's desk.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — sol-

root — sol-: to be accustomed, used to (Latin (solere))

suffix — -ence

suffix — -ence: state or quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Insolence combines in- ('not') with Latin solere ('to be accustomed') and -ence ('state or quality of') -- insolent behavior is literally 'unaccustomed' behavior, breaking the normal, expected rules of respect.

Use the root in a new word: obsolete

Use the root in a new word: obsolete: You may remember obsolete from earlier in this course -- ob- + solere means 'no longer practiced or in use,' the same root as insolence, just pointed at outdated things instead of rude people.

Word Choice

Insolence specifically describes disrespect toward someone owed courtesy or obedience -- a student to a teacher, an employee to a boss -- rather than rudeness between equals.
